newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine court mulls closing Israeli bomb case.
newsitem.headline: Argentine court mulls closing Israeli bomb case.

text.p: Argentina's Supreme Court is considering calling a halt to its fruitless investigation into the bomb attack on the Israeli embassy in 1992, which killed 29 people, said a court official on Monday.

"This possibility is being studied ... though that does not mean it will be closed," said a court official who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity. "Obviously opinion is divided among the members of the court."
The 1992 bomb attack reduced the city-centre embassy to rubble. Two years later, another bomb demolished a cultural centre of Buenos Aires' large Jewish community, killing 86 people.
To the outrage of Argentine Jews and Israel, after five years the police have not solved either case, though Israel has blamed Iranian-backed Moslem fundamentalists.
The only suspects being held are police officers and a car thief accused of providing the vehicle for the 1994 attack.

The official said Supreme Court members decided to study the option of giving up the probe after meeting last week with security forces and civil engineers who argued that the explosion came from within the diplomatic mission as opposed to the government's line that the explosion was a car bomb.
The official said some members of the court were so frustrated over the differing theories of the basics of the case that they felt the entire probe should be dropped.

The theory that the blast came from within the embassy has angered the Jewish community and caused tension between Israeli Ambassador Yitzhak Aviran and Supreme Court judges who thought it could be the work of right-wing Jewish groups.
"For now all we know is what the press is saying," said an Israeli embassy official. "The truth is we don't know what position to take. For the time being, all we can do is wait."

Sergio Widder, Argentine representative of the Wiesenthal Centre, a Jewish organisation that hunts Nazi war criminals, said he had doubts about the Supreme Court's will to continue the failed five-year investigation.
"But if the case is closed, it will be a major loss of credibility for the legal system," Widder told Reuters.
